title: the summit sit
hook: a glint in the wet sand at low tide, and a shell that was a shell the whole time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit stood in a crowded shelter with the Alvars, and their lamps of verse. Did you make room for one more somewhere crowded? Day one thousand four hundred nineteen.

Low tide, late afternoon. Something in the wet sand catches the sun and flashes, bright as a dropped coin. A walker bends down for it. It's a shell, the inside of it shining. Nothing about the shell changed when it was picked up. It was a shell the whole time. What changed was the seeing. Shankara chose very nearly this picture to open his commentary on the Brahma Sutras. Today's summit sit climbs back to the last stretch of the lineage track: jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A GLINT IN THE SAND.` → `ONLY A SHELL.` → `THE SEEING CHANGED.`

segments.voice: Before he comments on a single line of the Brahma Sutras, Shankara writes a preface about that shell: mother-of-pearl taken for silver, one thing mistaken for another. His teaching is that a mistake like this sits at the root of bondage: taking the body and the mind, which come and go, for the self. Gaudapada, in his verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, gives the same kind of picture. On a dim path, something real, a rope, is taken for something else, a snake. The fear is real. The snake isn't. And what ends the fear isn't fighting the snake or running from it. It's seeing. When the rope is seen as a rope, the snake doesn't leave. It was never there. The Brahma Sutras themselves open with a word that sounds almost casual: now. Now, then, the wish to know Brahman. And in his comment on the fourth sutra, Shankara says freedom isn't produced, the way a pot is made from clay. It's what is already so, uncovered, the way the shell was always a shell. Gaudapada's last picture is a firebrand whirled in the dark, drawing circles that aren't there. Hold the stick still, and the circles stop. From up here, jnana looks less like piling up information and more like a light coming on. Not everyone on the path reads it this way. Ramanuja, whom the year also read, holds the world and the selves in it as real, the body of God, not a mistake to be seen through. But on the jnana track, the work is this one: look closely enough, and what frightened you turns out to be rope.
screen: `THE SHELL TAKEN FOR SILVER.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `NOW, THEN, THE WISH TO KNOW.` · `THE FIREBRAND HELD STILL.` · then, large: `IT WAS ALWAYS ROPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring the light. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one worry that has been coiled on your path lately. Don't fight it. Just look at it more closely, the way a flashlight would. What, exactly, is there? What have you added in the dim light? Stay with plain seeing for a while. Then let the worry rest, and simply rest as the one who sees. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: jnana, the path of knowing, and the rope that was only ever rope. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, when your heart jumps at something, a message, a noise, a look, take one breath and look again before you run. Day one thousand four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta study the Upanishads, the Brahma Sutras and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher, and pair the study with reflection and meditation on what the self is.

glints like silver in Shankara's preface

myth: in Gaudapada's picture, the light makes the snake leave
the snake doesn't leave; it was never there. the light only shows the rope.

fork.setup: dusk, a garden path. a coil lies across the stones and your heart jumps. what ends the fear, in Gaudapada's picture?
options: bringing a light and seeing it's a rope.
fork.reveal: seeing ends it. once the rope is seen, the snake doesn't run away. it was never there to begin with.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: jñāna, knowing, the path of knowledge; pronunciation varies by region.

trapdoor: what you thought: jnana means learning lots of facts.
what it means: it's a seeing that ends a mistake, like a light showing the rope.
what a scholar hears: Shankara's preface on superimposition (adhyasa) before Brahma Sutra 1.1.1, and Gaudapada's rope-snake and firebrand in the Mandukya Karika.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 2.17–18 (the rope and the snake); 4.47–50 (the firebrand)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya, preface (adhyasa) and 1.1.1–1.1.4

notes: Summit sit, day 8: revisits 'jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)' (1232–1237) and 'the Mandukya Karika' (1238–1243), with a brief, unranked mention of Ramanuja (1226–1231).

Shankara's preface: shell-silver example of superimposition; 'at the root of bondage' paraphrases his presentation of adhyasa as the root of bondage; confirm phrasing. 'Freedom is not produced' follows his comment on 1.1.4; the height chart image is the year's own (1236).
Mandukya Karika: rope-snake at 2.17–18, firebrand (alata) at 4.47–50; confirm verse numbers.
Ramanuja's position summarized in one sentence ('the world and the self as real in their own right'); confirm it is fair to Vishishtadvaita.

Editor pass: the hook moved from a coiled rope on a path to a shell glinting in the sand (Shankara's own shell-and-silver), since 1413 had just opened on a coiled snake; teach reordered (preface, then rope and snake); the garbled 'taking what is limited and passing for the self' rewritten; 'again and again' cut; the height-chart line cut as unclear; Ramanuja's view restated as the world and selves real as God's body, not real 'in their own right'.
